Operation Pillar of Defense

Military Operation, Airstrikes, Civilian Casualties · 2012-11-14 · Escalation following targeted killing of Hamas military commander

2012-11-14
Date
Gaza Strip
Location
167 Palestinian, 6 Israeli
Deaths
Not documented
Displaced
Location, thenGaza Strip, Palestinian territory under Israeli blockade since 2007, governed by Hamas
Location, nowGaza Strip; Palestinian territory, Israeli-occupied since 1967, Hamas-governed since 2007; Under blockade; subject to recurring Israeli military operations
PerpetratorsIsrael Defense Forces (IDF); Israeli Air Force (IAF); Israeli Navy
ClassificationWar Crimes; Violations of IHL (B'Tselem May 2013 Report)

Summary

On November 14, 2012, at approximately 15:45, the Israeli Air Force assassinated Ahmed al-Jabari, head of Hamas's military wing, marking the start of Operation Pillar of Defense. Over eight days, the IDF struck approximately 1,500 targets across Gaza—including underground rocket launchers, arms-smuggling tunnels, weapons storage facilities, and residences of Hamas officials. Unlike Operation Cast Lead (2008-09), no ground incursion occurred.

According to B'Tselem's field investigations published May 2013, the operation killed 167 Palestinians: at least 87 civilians who did not participate in hostilities (52%), including 32 children; 62 combatants; 7 targets of assassinations; and 11 of unknown status. The UN Protection Cluster documented over 11,100 injuries, including 3,374 children. Analysis reveals 80% of civilian deaths occurred in the final four days, when the ratio of civilian to combatant deaths reversed sharply.

Six Israelis died from Palestinian rocket fire: four civilians and two security personnel. Palestinian groups fired 1,667 rockets toward Israel (ISA figures); 436 were intercepted by Iron Dome. Hamas also executed at least 6-7 Palestinians accused of collaboration during the operation. B'Tselem investigated nine specific incidents raising 'grave suspicions' of IHL violations, including attacks killing children working in fields, families in homes without warnings, and civilians during Arab foreign ministers' visit. The IDF Spokesperson initially admitted 'probable error' in strike killing 12 members of al-Dalu family, but MAG Corps later closed case without prosecution.

Timeline

October–Early November 2012
Pre-Operation Escalation
Four rounds of intensified violence: Palestinian rocket fire at southern Israel; Israeli incursions and airstrikes in Gaza. 23 Palestinians killed (7 civilians, 3 children); 93 Palestinians injured (77 civilians); 14 Israelis/foreign nationals injured (8 civilians). November 10-14: over 120 rockets fired from Gaza toward Israel.
UN OCHA Humanitarian Monitor (Oct-Nov 2012)
November 14, 2012, ~15:45
Operation Begins: Assassination of Ahmed al-Jabari
IAF airstrike targets vehicle in Gaza City, killing Ahmed al-Jabari (head of Hamas military wing, Al-Qassam Brigades) and passenger Muhammad al-Hams. This marked official start of Operation Pillar of Defense. Israeli officials cited 100+ rockets in prior 24 hours as justification.
B'Tselem Report (May 2013), pp. 23-24

Testimony

Muna a-Shawa
“My daughter Yusra, 18, was sitting watching television in our western room. I was standing by the window of the eastern room, next to Yusra's room, and was about to call my children...to come upstairs. At about 4:30 PM, before I had a chance to call them, I heard an explosion inside my apartment. I saw dust and debris flying everywhere. I felt pain. I took a few steps and took hold of Yusra's hand. She took half a step together with me and then fell down. I tried to find her but couldn't because of all the dust and debris. I called out to her but she didn't answer...My son Muhammad came to the door, grabbed me and took me down to the street. I said to him, 'Go find Yusra.' He told me she had been killed...but I wouldn't talk with anyone and said that I wanted Yusra. I wanted to see her and make sure that she was okay, but I could feel that she wasn't all right.”
B'Tselem Report (May 2013), pp. 24-25
Tamam al-'Asali
“After lunch on Wednesday, 21 November 2012, my husband Talal asked me to make tea for everyone. Talal went outside to a nearby area that he cultivates to pick some herbs for tea. Two of his children, his son Ayman and daughter 'Abir came along. I began preparing the things for tea when suddenly I heard a powerful explosion from behind the house. I went outside immediately and ran to the place where Talal and the children were. Even before I reached them, I could already see Talal and Ayman lying on the ground, covered in blood...I understood that my husband had apparently been killed instantaneously. Ayman was still moving a little bit. I didn't see my daughter 'Abir. I felt dizzy and weak. Then, apparently, I passed out. [Later told] that 'Abir had also been killed. I screamed and cried hysterically. Three members of my family killed at one blow. I lost them all in an instant, for no reason.”
B'Tselem Report (May 2013), pp. 26-27
Naji Qdeih
“At around 9:30 PM on 17 November 2012...I decided that we had best go over to the house of my first wife Maha, because it was better protected...I picked up my infant daughter and went over to Maha's house, just seven meters away. Then I returned to get some clothes and a blanket for Mayar. I asked Samaher to bring another blanket and join me. Samaher left the apartment carrying the blanket. Suddenly there was a huge explosion. Chunks of stone went flying all over the place. White smoke filled the courtyard...I found my wife Samaher lying on the ground near the steps of the balcony. I picked her up and saw that her left leg was severed and her clothes torn. Blood was trickling from her mouth. I picked her up and asked that she recite the Shehadatein prayer because I realized that she was badly injured and wouldn't survive. [Samaher died at scene]”
B'Tselem Report (May 2013), pp. 15-16
Sarah Abu Khusah
“At about 8:00 o'clock in the morning, three of my grandchildren were playing in front of the house, which is part of the house's compound...Suddenly we heard a huge explosion nearby. We all ran outside to see what happened. I was in shock when I saw that the spot that was hit was right next to the wall that encloses the house, and that it had actually destroyed the wall. I saw my grandson Iyad lying dead on the ground. He had been hit directly by shrapnel. Another of my grandsons, Suhaib, was lying on the ground beside him but he was moving. Sarah was also lying on the ground. I called for an ambulance right away and picked up Iyad. [Iyad, 18 months old, killed; Suhaib (6) and Sarah (4) critically injured]”
B'Tselem Report (May 2013), pp. 20-21
B'Tselem (institutional)
“Report conclusion (May 2013): 'The findings of this report raise grave suspicions of misconduct. However, the means at B'Tselem's disposal are too limited to determine whether or not the Israeli military acted in accordance with the law in the cases presented here...Determining this requires additional information held by the military, which it refuses to disclose. Therefore, we call upon the Israeli authorities to conduct an independent investigation...and to present the findings publicly and transparently.'”
B'Tselem Report (May 2013), p. 39
Amnesty International
“Statement to UN Human Rights Council (February 2013): The Israeli authorities investigations into alleged violations of international humanitarian law during Operation Pillar of Defense follow a familiar pattern of operational debriefings rather than independent criminal investigations. Such investigations lack the necessary independence and transparency required under international law. The pattern of impunity for violations during Israeli military operations in Gaza must end.'”
Amnesty International, Statement to UN HRC (February 2013)

Historical impact

Immediate Impact
Escalation Dynamics: Demonstrated shift in Israeli military doctrine post-Cast Lead (2008-09) toward shorter, air-focused operations, but with continued high civilian toll (52% of deaths)
Long-term Significance
Cycle of Violence: Established pattern repeated in 2014 (Protective Edge—far deadlier), 2021 (Guardian of the Walls), and 2023-24 (ongoing devastation). Each operation followed similar escalation triggers and justifications
Accountability
✘ Zero prosecutions of Israeli commanders or personnel despite 87 civilian deaths
Documentation Legacy
B'Tselem Report (May 2013): Gold-standard field investigation documenting nine cases with detailed witness testimonies, legal analysis, and contextual data
Immediate Impact
Regional Tensions: Arab and Turkish foreign ministers visited Gaza during operation (Nov 20), highlighting regional concern and attempting mediation
Long-term Significance
Impunity Precedent: Complete lack of prosecutions despite B'Tselem's documented evidence set precedent for future operations. MAG's 'operational debriefings' model continued
Accountability
✘ MAG Corps opened 70 inquiries; closed cases with minimal public information and 'no criminal offense found' determinations
Documentation Legacy
UN OCHA Humanitarian Monitors: Provided casualty figures, injury data, and humanitarian impact assessments during and after operation
Immediate Impact
Egypt's Role: President Mohamed Morsi brokered ceasefire, marking Egypt's post-Arab Spring involvement in Gaza diplomacy
Long-term Significance
Humanitarian Monitoring: Operation galvanized international human rights community; B'Tselem's May 2013 report became model for field investigation methodology in conflict zones
Accountability
✘ Amnesty International criticized MAG investigations as 'operational debriefings' lacking independence (Feb 2013 UN HRC statement)
Documentation Legacy
Al Mezan Center for Human Rights: Parallel Palestinian documentation efforts; submitted cases to ICC Prosecutor (though Palestine not yet member state)
Immediate Impact
Tactical Shift: First major combat deployment of Iron Dome missile defense system—intercepted 436/1,667 rockets (26%), reducing Israeli casualties relative to rocket volume
Long-term Significance
Legal Discourse: B'Tselem's critique of 'overly broad' military target definitions and inadequate warnings influenced IHL advocacy and academic discourse on proportionality
Accountability
✘ B'Tselem's nine case investigations raising 'grave suspicions' of IHL violations produced no substantive responses beyond vague MAG letters
Documentation Legacy
Methodology: B'Tselem's investigation model—field researchers, named witnesses (with consent), legal IHL analysis, submission to MAG, documentation of MAG responses—became template
Immediate Impact
Blockade Tightening: Operation reinforced Gaza's isolation; ceasefire did not address blockade, which continued
Long-term Significance
Palestinian Trauma: Added to cumulative trauma of Gaza population; families interviewed months later remained in shock and grief
Accountability
✘ Al-Dalu case: Despite IDF admission of 'probable error' killing 12 (5 children, 5 women), MAG closed case claiming 'efforts to minimize harm'—no explanation for why efforts failed
Accountability
✘ Iyad Abu Khusah case: MAG denied strike occurred despite documented death and injuries—exemplifies accountability crisis
Accountability
✘ No reparations paid to families; property damage through Israeli-administered compensation system with delays
Accountability
✘ Pattern established: Military investigates itself, provides minimal public information, closes cases, no external oversight
